extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry/literature
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging or composing metrical poetry, focused on the proper relation of metre, diction, imagery, and imaginative activity, and on how poetic language should differ from prose. Includes stylistic warnings (prosaism, incongruous imagery) and governing principles (grammar, logic, taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre must be accompanied by the natural language of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: “as the elements of metre owe their existence to a state of increased excitement, so the metre itself should be accompanied by the natural language of excitement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metre originates from a balance in the mind between passion and restraint; therefore metrical language ought to reflect an excited state of feeling. Poetic diction should show that intensity rather than adopting flat, neutral prose diction. Examples: the poet’s language must match the heightened emotional pulse that creates metre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traces of present volition should be discernible in metrical language
rubrics_metrics.description: “as these elements are formed into metre artificially, by a voluntary act... so the traces of present volition should throughout the metrical language be proportionately discernible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry involves a conscious shaping (will/judgment) of passion for the sake of pleasure; readers should be able to perceive this shaping. The poet’s deliberate choices (cadences, figures, emphasis) should be present rather than wholly spontaneous or mechanical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union/interpenetration of passion and will
rubrics_metrics.description: “There must be not only a partnership, but a union; an interpenetration of passion and of will, of spontaneous impulse and of voluntary purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective verse reconciles spontaneous feeling and conscious artistic control. Either extreme (unrestrained passion without craft, or cold technical art without feeling) undermines poetry. The critic should expect a balance — imaginative energy shaped by judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent use of picturesque and vivifying language and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: “this union... tends to produce a more frequent employment of picturesque and vivifying language, than would be natural in any other case...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry normally employs a higher density of striking images and figures than didactic or argumentative prose. Such devices are originally offspring of passion but become adopted tools of power; their kind, frequency and occasion must suit the poetic excitement and not be arbitrary ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of matter and thought to metrical form
rubrics_metrics.description: “Where, therefore, correspondent food and appropriate matter are not provided for the attention and feelings thus roused there must needs be a disappointment felt... ”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metre stimulates attention and expectation; if the subject matter or diction cannot sustain that stimulation, metre becomes a disappointment. Poets should choose material and expressions that justify and reward metrical emphasis (avoid trivial or mismatched content).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre is conditional and must combine with other poetic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: “metre itself is simply a stimulant of the attention... this we have shown to be conditional, and dependent on the appropriateness of the thoughts and expressions, to which the metrical form is superadded.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter alone does not make poetry. Criticism should assess the combination of metre with thought, feeling, diction and imagery; a metrical surface without corresponding poetic substance is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosaism — lines that read indistinguishably as prose
rubrics_metrics.description: “The existence of prosaisms, and that they detract from the merit of a poem, must at length be conceded, when a number of successive lines can be rendered... unrecognizable as verse, or as having even been intended for verse, by simply transcribing them as prose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If successive lines can be transcribed into prose without loss, the poem has become prosaic and loses poetic merit. This applies to blank verse and rhyme: if small edits render it plain prose, the verse-form is only visual, not substantive. Avoid writing where metre is only 'to the eye.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of poetic diction from ordinary conversational prose
rubrics_metrics.description: “The true question must be, whether there are not modes of expression... which are in their fit and natural place in a serious prose composition, but would be disproportionate and heterogeneous in metrical poetry; and, vice versa...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and poets should judge whether particular constructions, orders of sentences, and figures of speech are appropriate to poetic contexts. Some expressions suit prose but jar in verse; others belong to poetry. Sensitivity to these differences is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery must be congruous and make good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Gray: a line is bad “because it conveys incongruous images; because it confounds the cause and the effect; the real thing with the personified representative of the thing; in short, because it differs from the language of good sense!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor or hackneyed mythological personifications, confused causal relations, or schoolboy images make lines bad — not merely because they differ from prose, but because they violate good sense and congruity. Poetic diction must maintain logical clarity of imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should regulate style by grammar, logic, psychology, and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: “By the principles of grammar, logic, psychology. In one word by such a knowledge of the facts, material and spiritual, that most appertain to his art... and acquires the name of Taste.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than imitating colloquial speech blindly, poets should ground their diction in sound principles of language and human psychology; cultivated knowledge and taste enable proper discrimination of style. This is presented as the rule-based (but principled) side of poetic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic language should arise from imagination/meditation, not slavish copying of vulgar speech
rubrics_metrics.description: “Is it obtained by wandering about in search of angry or jealous people in uncultivated society, in order to copy their words? Or not far rather by the power of imagination proceeding upon the all in each of human nature? By meditation, rather than by observation?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's proper source is imaginative insight and universal human nature; mere transcription of colloquial or rustic speech is not sufficient justification for poetic diction. Use of rustic language must be justified by imaginative truth, not mere mimicry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and harmonious adjustment of parts to essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: “the high spiritual instinct of the human being impelling us to seek unity by harmonious adjustment, and thus establishing the principle that all the parts of an organized whole must be assimilated to the more important and essential parts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems should exhibit organic unity; peripheral parts must be assimilated to the essential core (theme, tone, principal features). The critic should expect harmonious adjustment across parts rather than disjointed or mismatched passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of metre being merely regular/visible while diction is capricious
rubrics_metrics.description: Response to Wordsworth's claim: rhyme/metre are “regular and uniform, and not, like that produced by... poetic diction, arbitrary, and subject to infinite caprices...”; the essay counters that capricious diction can as easily ruin metre as wild minds can ruin rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regularity of metre does not excuse arbitrary or capricious diction. The poet is not absolved from exercising taste and judgement simply because meter is a fixed framework; metre can be misused and thereby fail to secure aesthetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty or trivial subject-matter that metre cannot dignify
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that lines are not bad because unpoetic but because “they are empty of all sense and feeling; and that it were an idle attempt to prove that ‘an ape is not a Newton’... ”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter and poetic devices cannot redeem trivial or empty content. A poet must supply genuine feeling and sense; otherwise even correctly metrical lines remain worthless despite poetic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of poetic imagination are internal and cannot be rigidly prescribed
rubrics_metrics.description: “Could a rule be given from without, poetry would cease to be poetry, and sink into a mechanical art... The rules of the Imagination are themselves the very powers of growth and production.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While principles (grammar, taste, logic) guide the poet, rigid external formulas for poetic diction are inappropriate. Genuine poetic practice depends on internal imaginative rules and parental instinct of genius; criticism aims to articulate principles but not reduce poetry to mechanical rules.
